catalog_quote: [p. 59] O acento em Terena pode manifestar-se em uma das três primeiras sílabas. Limitação essa, denominada de “Restrição da Janela de Três Sílabas”, segundo a qual, o acento alcança maximamente a terceira sílaba a contar da borda esquerda da palavra (Kager, 1993). [...] [p. 62] Os dados dos padrões acentuais acima nos informa que o acento da língua é não previsível. Hipotetizamos que o acento da língua é livre, ou seja, já previamente definido no léxico. Por outro lado, o sistema acentual da língua sinaliza estar também governado por fatores morfológicos. Por exemplo, os diferentes padrões acentuais (2/3 – 1/3 – 1/2) parecem interagir com as diferentes classes de raízes (verbal ou nominal). Além do mais o acento demonstra ser cíclico. Ele se manifesta na raiz (1a posição) e depois se desloca em direção à borda direita da palavra (2a posição) quando são acrescidos sufixos tais como –ti …
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Language not in the catalog. Both Glottolog stress-title items are by Bendor-Samuel and neither could be opened: 'Stress in Terena' (TPS 61, 1962/63, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-968x.1962.tb00995.x) is Wiley-paywalled behind an automated-access block with no repository copy (Crossref/OpenAlex records saved), and 'Some prosodic features in Terena' (In Memory of J. R. Firth, 1966, pp. 30-39) exists only as an unavailable archive.org lending item. Its content is recoverable second-hand: Silva 2009 (cap. V) translates Bendor-Samuel's core claim that non-particle words are stressed on one of two syllables within the first three, the choice being grammatical, not phonological; Martins 2009 (p. 59, p. 62) gives the best first-hand statement read here (three-syllable left-edge window, lexically free but morphologically shifted two-position stress, acute vs circumflex accent types), and Ferreira 2021 (pp. 17-22) confirms morphologically conditioned shift from speaker checks. Priority: high for acquiring Bendor-Samuel 1962 (the primary description); medium for 1966 (possibly Firthian prosodies rather than word stress).

new_statements.translation: [p. 59] Stress in Terena may appear on any one of the first three syllables. This limitation, called the 'Three-Syllable Window Restriction', means stress reaches at most the third syllable counting from the left edge of the word (Kager 1993). [...] [p. 62] The data on the stress patterns above tell us that the stress of the language is not predictable. We hypothesise that stress is free, i.e. already specified in the lexicon. On the other hand, the stress system also appears to be governed by morphological factors. [...] Moreover stress proves to be cyclic: it appears on the root (1st position) and then shifts toward the right edge of the word (2nd position) when suffixes such as -ti and -na are added.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (accent) falls on one of the first three syllables of the word; which of them is not phonologically predictable but lexically specified per root class and manipulated by morphology: each noun/verb has a '1st position' (root form, e.g. with definite possessor / one TAM value) and a '2nd position' one syllable to the right (with suffixes -ti 'unspecified possessor', -na, etc.), giving patterns 2~3, 1~3, 1~2. The accent comes in two phonetic types: acento I (acute: level pitch, gemination of the following consonant) and acento II (circumflex: falling pitch, lengthened vowel), themselves grammatically contrastive (íti 'blood' vs îti 'you'; pího 'when he went' vs pîho 'he went'). The final syllable is normally unstressed (extrametrical); a handful of nouns (with final glottal stop) and some verb forms carry word-final accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Martins builds weight-insensitive left-headed binary feet (syllabic trochees) bidirectionally outward from the lexically placed primary, degenerate feet banned, final stray syllable extrametrical (abstract p. 7; §4.6.5 pp. 69-71); Silva 2009 p. 90 notes most words have a primary and a secondary stress. No independent acoustic verification of secondaries.
new_statements.exceptions: Particles are outside the system (Bendor-Samuel apud Silva 2009 p. 87); a few nouns and di-/trisyllabic verbs have final stress (§4.6.6 pp. 71-72); Portuguese loans often keep their accent and do not shift under suffixation (Ferreira 2021 p. 22); prefix ko- 'causative' attracts the accent leftward (Ferreira 2021).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (morphological) word in citation/elicited forms; Martins §4.6.6-4.7 and Carvalho 2017 (apud Ferreira 2021 p. 21) note phrase-level and intonational melodies can alter the basic word profile (e.g. verb+object, noun+possessor take acento II on the 2nd syllable at phonological-phrase level). Whether the prominence is 'stress', 'tone' or 'pitch accent' is disputed: Aikhenvald 1999/2001 and Souza 2008 (Kinikinau) suspect tone; Butler 1977 speaks of two tones on one of the first three syllables; Carvalho 2021 calls it a 'tonal accent'; Martins 2009, Silva 2009, Butler 2001 treat it as accentual.
new_statements.identity_note: Martins 2009 and Silva 2009 describe Terena proper as spoken at Aldeia Cachoeirinha (Miranda, MS). Souza 2008 describes the Kinikinau variety (Aldeia São João, Bodoquena; Glottolog dialect kini1234 under tere1279) and explicitly does not mark accent, suspecting tone. Carvalho 2016 argues Terena, Chané, Guaná and Kinikinau are one language.

new_statements.reading: Lexically unpredictable (free) stress confined to a left-edge three-syllable window; each noun/verb has two grammatically distinct stress positions (root-based 1st position on syllable 1 or 2; 2nd position one syllable further right, on syllable 2 or 3, under suffixation), realised with two accent types (acute vs circumflex). Martins analyses it metrically as left-headed syllabic trochees with final-syllable extrametricality. Ferreira 2021 (pp. 17-22, own speaker checks) agrees the shift is morphologically conditioned (rightward under -ti/-na/-xo/-mo suffixation, leftward under prefixation) and Silva 2009 attributes the same two-position, grammatically determined placement to Bendor-Samuel 1962; Aikhenvald's tonal hypothesis is rejected by Martins and Silva, left open by Ferreira.

sources.quote: [Silva 2009, paraphrasing Bendor-Samuel 'Stress in Terena', fn. 20] "De acordo com Bendor-Samuel (1963b), há um contraste na colocação do acento em palavras (exceto partículas) que são acentuadas em uma das duas, exceto as primeiras três sílabas da palavra. A seleção da primeira ou segunda dessas duas sílabas acentuadas tem funções gramaticais importantes; algumas vezes, por exemplo, o acento distingue o sujeito do objeto. [...] Essa seleção entre as duas sílabas acentuais não é previsível com nenhuma base fonológica [...] unicamente determinada por fatores gramaticais" (EN: according to B-S, words other than particles are stressed on one of two of the first three syllables; choice between the two is grammatically, not phonologically, determined).
sources.locator: Full text not opened. Content known only through Silva 2009, cap. V 'O acento' (PDF pp. 86-87, fn. 20 'Tradução nossa'), Martins 2009 §4.2 p. 59, Ferreira 2021 pp. 15-17.
sources.note: Per the secondary reports (not the article itself): every Terena word except particles has stress on one of two syllables lying within the first three syllables of the word; which of the two positions is used is not phonologically predictable but is set by morphology/syntax (e.g. it can distinguish subject from object); where that positional contrast is neutralised, a contrast between two sets of phonetic exponents of stress (the acute vs circumflex 'accent I/II') carries the grammatical contrast. Martins 2009 p. 59 cites the same paper for 'one of the first three syllables' and for Terena be…
